trauma.title: Multi-Trauma from RTC - Motorcycle vs Car
trauma.callReason: Motorcycle accident, rider on ground not moving
trauma.sceneDescription: Busy highway, motorcycle lying on side, car with front damage
trauma.sceneImageCaption: Motorcycle vs car collision on Sheikh Zayed Road
trauma.appearance: Blood on face, right leg deformed, unconscious
trauma.generalImpression: Young male, supine on road, helmet removed by bystanders
managementImmediate: Scene safety and PPE

CATASTROPHIC HAEMORRHAGE FIRST — CAT tourniquet 5-7cm proximal to open femur bleed (not over joint), note time; wound-pack arterial bleeds — this is step 1 of MARCH, before airway (exsanguination kills faster than airway failure in first minutes)
Manual C-spine stabilisation (selective — rigid collar only if mechanism + midline tenderness + neuro deficit)
Airway management (suction, jaw thrust, OPA/LMA/ETT)
High-flow oxygen and BVM if needed — aim SpO2 ≥94% (TBI protective)
Needle decompression if tension pneumothorax suspected (5th ICS AAL, 14G x 8cm preferred per TCCC 2022)
IV access x2 large bore (14-16G)
Small-volume Hartmann's aliquots (250mL) titrated — target SBP ≥110 mmHg if TBI (BTF 4th Ed; old SBP >90 is outdated), SBP 80-90 if penetrating without TBI

Head elevated 30 degrees
Mannitol 0.25-1g/kg or hypertonic saline if herniation suspected
trauma.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Severe TBI with signs of herniation

trauma.title: Penetrating Chest Wound
trauma.callReason: Stab wound to chest, bleeding heavily
managementImmediate: Apply vented chest seal (HyFin Vent / Russell / SAM) — TCCC 2022 / PHTLS 10 standard. Improvised 3-sided taped dressings are unreliable (fail when wet/bloody) and no longer first-line.
High-flow oxygen 15L/min
IV access x2 large-bore (14-16G)

PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION target SBP 80-90 mmHg (penetrating, no TBI): 250mL Hartmann's aliquots titrated to radial pulse / mentation — avoid large crystalloid volumes (dilutional coagulopathy). Activate Major Haemorrhage Protocol for blood products.
TRANEXAMIC ACID 1g IV slow push over 10 min within 3h of injury (CRASH-2, JRCALC 2024) — then 1g infusion over 8h in-hospital.
Position patient with injured side down if possible
Prepare for tension pneumothorax development — be ready to burp the seal or needle-decompress

Prepare for emergency thoracotomy
Rapid transport to trauma center
trauma.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Cardiac Tamponade secondary to penetrating chest trauma
keyObservations: Beck's Triad: Hypotension, JVD, Muffled heart sounds
Signs of shock: tachycardia, poor perfusion, altered mental status
Pulsus paradoxus: >10mmHg drop in BP during inspiration
redFlags: Cardiac tamponade - clinical diagnosis, DO NOT wait for confirmation
Patient rapidly deteriorating toward cardiac arrest
Possible cardiac injury based on wound location

Pre-alert trauma center

managementImmediate: High-flow oxygen 15L/min via non-rebreather

Immediate needle decompression — PREFERRED site 4th-5th ICS anterior-to-mid axillary line (TCCC 2022); 2nd ICS mid-clavicular is a valid alternate but fails in >30% of adults (chest-wall thickness, great-vessel proximity)

trauma.generalImpression: Young male, pale, holding the bleeding stump of his right forearm
managementImmediate: Haemorrhage control — apply tourniquet 5-7cm proximal to amputation site; apply tight with one-handed windlass; note time applied
Direct pressure to stump if tourniquet not immediately available — use haemostatic dressing (QuikClot, Celox)

Fluid resuscitation 500mL NS bolus — reassess BP; target SBP >90
Preserve the amputated part: wrap in moist sterile gauze, place in sealed waterproof bag, then place bag in container of ice water — do NOT place directly on ice or submerge in water
Label the bag with patient name, time of amputation, and time placed on ice
Analgesia — Morphine 0.1mg/kg IV titrated; Ketamine 0.3mg/kg IV if haemodynamically compromised
Reassess tourniquet effectiveness — proximal pulse should be absent, bleeding should be controlled

burns.title: Burns - Industrial Fire with Inhalation Injury
burns.location: Industrial area in Jebel Ali, Dubai
burns.callReason: Factory fire, multiple people trapped, one with severe burns
burns.sceneDescription: Industrial factory with active fire, smoke throughout building, patient found near exit
burns.appearance: Burns to face/neck/chest/arms, soot marks around nose/mouth
burns.generalImpression: Adult male with extensive burns, conscious but in pain, coughing
managementImmediate: Stop the burning process — remove from heat source, remove smouldering clothing and jewellery (will continue to burn and become constricting as oedema forms)

Cool the burn with cool (NOT cold) running water for 20 minutes if within 3 hours of injury — cooling limited to burn site only; actively WARM the rest of the patient (hypothermia + large TBSA = lethal triad)
Dress with loose cling film applied lengthwise (never circumferential — constricts as oedema forms). Do NOT use wet dressings on large TBSA (hypothermia risk)
Assess airway - early intubation if soot around mouth/nose, hoarseness/stridor, facial burns, or singed nasal hairs
100% oxygen via non-rebreather (treat CO/CN poisoning)
IV access x2 with large-bore catheters
Fluid resuscitation: Parkland formula (4ml x weight(kg) x %TBSA, half in first 8 hours, half in next 16 hours)
Cover burns with sterile, dry, non-adherent dressing
burns.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Major Thermal Burns with Inhalation Injury
keyObservations: Face/neck/chest burns - high risk for airway

burns.title: Electrical Burn with Cardiac Arrest
burns.sceneDescription: Building site, patient near electrical panel
managementImmediate: SCENE SAFETY FIRST — do NOT approach until power source is confirmed OFF by facility electrician/engineer; call for power isolation
Once safe: begin CPR immediately — high-quality chest compressions 100-120/min, depth 5-6cm
Attach AED/defibrillator immediately — electrical arrests are frequently VF and highly shockable
Defibrillation per ALS protocol — 200J biphasic for VF/pVT
Advanced airway — RSI or supraglottic airway; electrical burns can cause airway oedema rapidly
IV/IO access — large bore bilateral antecubital fossa
Adrenaline 1mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes per ALS algorithm
Examine for entry and exit wounds — entry typically at contact point (hands), exit where current left body (feet)

managementImmediate: Immediate CPR on firm surface - 30:2 ratio, depth 5-6cm, rate 100-120/min, optimize hand position and body position (AHA 2025)
AED/defibrillator application and rhythm analysis
Defibrillation if VF/pVT (150-200J biphasic)

allSummaries.title: Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response
allSummaries.callReason: Palpitations and dizziness
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Office environment, patient at desk
allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged female, anxious, uncomfortable
managementImmediate: Assess hemodynamic stability — BP, GCS, chest pain, signs of shock
Obtain 12-lead ECG to confirm rhythm
IV access x1 (18G)
If UNSTABLE (SBP <90, chest pain, GCS <14): Synchronized cardioversion 100-200J biphasic with procedural sedation

If STABLE: prehospital focus is continuous monitoring, IV access, identifying precipitants (infection, PE, dehydration, thyroid, alcohol). IV rate-control agents (metoprolol 5mg IV or diltiazem 0.25mg/kg IV) are administered in ED under cardiac monitoring — not routinely within UK JRCALC / UAE DCAS paramedic scope.
Oxygen if SpO2 <94%
Check anticoagulation status — warfarin/DOAC compliance

Immediate needle decompression — PREFERRED site is 4th-5th ICS anterior-to-mid axillary line per TCCC 2022 (2nd ICS mid-clavicular fails in >30% of adults due to chest-wall thickness and risks vessel injury)
Use 14G x 8cm catheter (5cm catheters demonstrably fail in ~1/3 of adults)
IV access + small-volume fluid challenges titrated to radial pulse (avoid large crystalloid boluses)
Continuous monitoring — reassess after decompression for recurrence
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Tension Pneumothorax

allSummaries.title: COPD Exacerbation
allSummaries.callReason: Increased breathlessness, using oxygen at home
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Small apartment, patient in armchair
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly male, barrel chest, using accessory muscles
managementImmediate: Controlled oxygen 24-28% via Venturi mask (target SpO2 88-92%)
Nebulized bronchodilators: Salbutamol 5mg + Ipratropium 500mcg
IV hydrocortisone 100mg
IV access
Position upright with tripod posture

allSummaries.title: Pulmonary Embolism
allSummaries.callReason: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Hotel room, patient on bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged female, anxious, dyspneic
managementImmediate: High-flow oxygen 15L/min via non-rebreather
IV access x2 (16-18G)
12-lead ECG (assess for S1Q3T3, right heart strain)
Fluid resuscitation if hypotensive (250-500ml crystalloid bolus)
Position semi-upright if comfortable

allSummaries.title: Multi-Trauma from RTC - Motorcycle vs Car
allSummaries.callReason: Motorcycle accident, rider on ground not moving
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Busy highway, motorcycle lying on side, car with front damage
allSummaries.sceneImageCaption: Motorcycle vs car collision on Sheikh Zayed Road
allSummaries.appearance: Blood on face, right leg deformed, unconscious
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, supine on road, helmet removed by bystanders
managementImmediate: Scene safety and PPE

CATASTROPHIC HAEMORRHAGE FIRST — CAT tourniquet 5-7cm proximal to open femur bleed (not over joint), note time; wound-pack arterial bleeds — this is step 1 of MARCH, before airway (exsanguination kills faster than airway failure in first minutes)
Manual C-spine stabilisation (selective — rigid collar only if mechanism + midline tenderness + neuro deficit)
Airway management (suction, jaw thrust, OPA/LMA/ETT)
High-flow oxygen and BVM if needed — aim SpO2 ≥94% (TBI protective)
Needle decompression if tension pneumothorax suspected (5th ICS AAL, 14G x 8cm preferred per TCCC 2022)
IV access x2 large bore (14-16G)
Small-volume Hartmann's aliquots (250mL) titrated — target SBP ≥110 mmHg if TBI (BTF 4th Ed; old SBP >90 is outdated), SBP 80-90 if penetrating without TBI
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Multi-trauma with TBI

allSummaries.title: Head Injury with Skull Fracture
allSummaries.callReason: Fall from height, head injury, unconscious
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Construction site, patient on ground
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, supine, blood around head
managementImmediate: C-spine immobilization with rigid collar and blocks
Airway management with cervical spine precautions (suction, jaw thrust)
High-flow oxygen
IV access x2 with isotonic fluids (Normal Saline only)
Hyperventilation (ETCO2 30-35 mmHg) if signs of herniation
Head elevated 30 degrees
Mannitol 0.25-1g/kg or hypertonic saline if herniation suspected
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Severe TBI with signs of herniation

allSummaries.title: Penetrating Chest Wound
allSummaries.callReason: Stab wound to chest, bleeding heavily
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Street corner, police present
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, sitting, holding chest
managementImmediate: Apply vented chest seal (HyFin Vent / Russell / SAM) — TCCC 2022 / PHTLS 10 standard. Improvised 3-sided taped dressings are unreliable (fail when wet/bloody) and no longer first-line.
High-flow oxygen 15L/min
IV access x2 large-bore (14-16G)

PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION target SBP 80-90 mmHg (penetrating, no TBI): 250mL Hartmann's aliquots titrated to radial pulse / mentation — avoid large crystalloid volumes (dilutional coagulopathy). Activate Major Haemorrhage Protocol for blood products.
TRANEXAMIC ACID 1g IV slow push over 10 min within 3h of injury (CRASH-2, JRCALC 2024) — then 1g infusion over 8h in-hospital.
Position patient with injured side down if possible
Prepare for tension pneumothorax development — be ready to burp the seal or needle-decompress
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Open Pneumothorax (Sucking Chest Wound)

allSummaries.title: Acute Ischemic Stroke - FAST Positive
allSummaries.callReason: Husband suddenly cannot speak or move right side
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Living room, patient in armchair
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly male, slumped in chair, facial droop obvious
managementImmediate: Perform FAST assessment
Establish exact time last known well (critical for thrombolysis)
Check blood glucose to rule out hypoglycemia
IV access (18-20G)
NPO - do not give food or drink
Continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring
Document baseline GCS and neurological findings
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Acute Ischemic Stroke

allSummaries.title: Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure
allSummaries.callReason: Daughter having a seizure, just stopped
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Bedroom, patient on bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, post-ictal, confused
managementImmediate: Position in recovery (lateral) position to protect airway
Suction oropharynx if blood/secretions present
High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
Check blood glucose immediately
IV access (18-20G)
Monitor vital signs
Midazolam 5-10mg IV/IM/IN if seizure recurs or >5 min (status epilepticus)
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure (Post-ictal)

allSummaries.title: Meningitis
allSummaries.callReason: Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Bedroom, patient in bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, photophobia, uncomfortable
managementImmediate: Benzylpenicillin 1.2g IM/IV (adult) — UK JRCALC / NICE CG102 prehospital first-line for suspected meningococcal disease with non-blanching rash (in every UK ambulance drug bag; ceftriaxone 2g IV reserved for hospital or penicillin-allergic alternative). Do NOT delay transport to give antibiotics.
IV access with large-bore cannula
Fluid resuscitation 30ml/kg if septic shock
High-flow oxygen (target SpO2 ≥94%)
Check blood glucose
Dexamethasone 10mg IV WITH or JUST BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (blunts cytokine response at bacterial lysis — loses benefit if given after)
Droplet precautions (FFP3 mask, eye protection, gloves)
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Bacterial Meningitis (Meningococcal)

allSummaries.title: Severe Hypoglycemia
allSummaries.callReason: Father confused and sweating, not responding properly
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Bedroom, patient on floor beside bed
allSummaries.position: Sitting on floor, leaning against bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged male, diaphoretic, confused
managementImmediate: Check blood glucose immediately (do not delay for history)
If conscious and cooperative: Oral glucose 15-20g (glucose tablets, sugary drink)
If impaired consciousness or unable to swallow: IV dextrose 10% 200-250ml or D50 50ml
If no IV access: Glucagon 1mg IM/SC
Recheck glucose in 10-15 minutes
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Severe Hypoglycemia

allSummaries.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
allSummaries.callReason: Vomiting, abdominal pain, breathing fast
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Living room, patient on sofa
allSummaries.appearance: Flushed, dry skin, acetone breath odor
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, Kussmaul breathing, drowsy
managementImmediate: IV access with large-bore cannula (14-16G)
Fluid resuscitation: 0.9% NaCl 1L over first hour (fluid FIRST, then insulin). Second litre over next 2h.
Check and document blood glucose and ketones (capillary + urine)

DO NOT give insulin bolus prehospital. Hospital pathway: fixed-rate insulin INFUSION 0.1 units/kg/hr ONLY after first litre of saline is running (UK JBDS 2023 — bolus insulin is associated with cerebral oedema, especially in young patients). Do not start insulin prehospital if transport <30 min.
Potassium replacement when K+ is 3.5-5.5 mmol/L (add 40 mmol KCl to fluids); if K+ <3.5, senior review (UK JBDS threshold, not <5.3)
Continuous cardiac monitoring for hypokalaemia-related arrhythmia
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Diabetic Ketoacidosis

allSummaries.title: Panic Attack with Hyperventilation
allSummaries.callReason: Wife having panic attack, cannot breathe, chest pain
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Living room, patient pacing
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, hyperventilating, distressed
managementImmediate: Ensure scene safety and remove from stressors if possible
Calm, reassuring communication — steady voice, slow breathing coaching
Full vital signs including SpO2 and blood glucose
12-lead ECG — mandatory for first presentation or atypical features to exclude cardiac cause
Coach controlled breathing — 4 counts in, hold 2, 6 counts out
Do NOT use paper bag — risk of dangerous hypoxia
IV access and oxygen only if organic cause not excluded
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Panic Attack

allSummaries.title: Elderly Fall with Hip Fracture
allSummaries.callReason: Mother fell in bathroom, cannot get up, leg looks wrong
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Bathroom floor, wet surface
allSummaries.position: Supine, left leg externally rotated and shortened
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly female, supine on bathroom floor, distressed
managementImmediate: Scene safety and request additional resources if needed for extrication from bathroom
Primary survey — check airway, breathing, circulation; assess for head injury from fall
Do not move patient until injury assessed — logroll or spinal precautions if indicated
Analgesia early — morphine 2-5mg IV titrated or consider fascia iliaca compartment block (FICB)
IV access (18G)
Immobilise fracture in position found — traction splint contraindicated for NOF fractures
Full exposure and secondary survey — check for other injuries (wrist, ribs, head)
Document anticoagulant use — warfarin/DOAC patients at elevated intracranial haemorrhage risk
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Neck of Femur Fracture

allSummaries.title: Post-Op Wound Infection
allSummaries.callReason: Surgical wound red and draining pus, fever
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Living room, patient on sofa
allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged male, uncomfortable, feverish
managementImmediate: Full sepsis screen — assess qSOFA (RR, BP, GCS): any ≥2 = sepsis, activate sepsis pathway
Full vital signs including temperature — fever >38°C or hypothermia <36°C both indicate systemic response
IV access (18G) — for antibiotics and fluids
IV fluid bolus 500mL NS if signs of sepsis-induced hypotension (SBP <100)
Blood glucose check — diabetes impairs wound healing and immune response; high BGL common
Assess wound: erythema, warmth, swelling, discharge, wound dehiscence, crepitus (gas in tissues = necrotising fasciitis)
Sterile dressing — cover wound to prevent further contamination
Analgesia — Paracetamol 1g IV or Morphine for severe pain
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Surgical Site Infection

allSummaries.title: Chest Pain - Rule Out ACS
allSummaries.callReason: Chest pain, worried it might be heart attack
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Modern apartment, patient at desk
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, anxious, no acute distress
managementImmediate: Full vital signs — BP, HR, RR, SpO2, BGL
12-lead ECG immediately — mandatory for all chest pain regardless of age or presentation
Detailed OPQRST pain history — onset, quality, radiation, severity, timing
Cardiovascular risk factor assessment — family history, smoking, diabetes, hypertension
Aspirin 300mg PO if not contraindicated — low threshold in first presentations
IV access if ECG abnormal or high-risk features identified
Serial 12-lead ECG at 15 minutes if initial ECG normal
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Musculoskeletal Chest Pain
redFlags: Atypical MI can present this way

allSummaries.title: Syncope - First Episode
allSummaries.location: Office building in Business Bay, Dubai
allSummaries.callReason: Employee fainted at work, now awake but confused
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Office floor, patient on chair
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, pale, recovering from syncope
managementImmediate: Scene safety
Supine positioning with legs elevated
Assess for injuries from fall
Blood glucose check
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Vasovagal Syncope

allSummaries.title: Heat Exhaustion
allSummaries.callReason: Worker dizzy and nauseated at construction site
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Outdoor construction site, direct sun
allSummaries.sceneImageCaption: Construction site in summer heat — Dubai
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young male, profuse sweating, weak
managementImmediate: Remove from hot environment — move to shaded or air-conditioned area immediately
Remove excess clothing to maximise surface cooling
Active cooling — cool wet cloths to skin, fan, ice packs to axillae and groin
Oral rehydration if conscious and tolerating — cool water or sports drink
IV access — Normal Saline 0.9% 500mL over 30 minutes if unable to tolerate oral fluids
Core temperature measurement — tympanic or axillary (rectal preferred if available)
Check blood glucose
Vital signs — assess for progression to heat stroke
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Heat Exhaustion

allSummaries.title: Pregnancy - Third Trimester Bleeding (Placenta Previa)
allSummaries.callReason: Pregnant woman, heavy vaginal bleeding, 34 weeks pregnant
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Master bedroom, patient lying on left side on bed
allSummaries.bystanders: Husband present, mother-in-law in other room
allSummaries.appearance: Pale, diaphoretic, visible blood on bedding
allSummaries.generalImpression: Pregnant female, pale, anxious, gripping abdomen
managementImmediate: Place patient in left lateral position to prevent aortocaval compression
High-flow oxygen 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask
IV access x2 with large-bore catheters (14-16G)
Fluid resuscitation: Normal Saline or Plasma-Lyte 500-1000ml bolus
Monitor vital signs and fetal heart rate if equipment available
NPO status - prepare for potential emergency surgery
Reassure patient and family
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Placenta Previa
keyObservations: Stable vital signs with mild tachycardia
redFlags: Potential placental abruption if bleeding increases

allSummaries.title: Pediatric - 3-Year-Old with Fever and Seizure
allSummaries.callReason: Child having seizure, very hot, mother screaming
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Living room, child on carpet, grandmother trying to help
allSummaries.appearance: Flushed, hot skin, eyes closed, twitching
allSummaries.generalImpression: Small child, post-ictal, hot to touch
managementImmediate: Airway management — place in lateral (recovery) position if post-ictal; do NOT insert objects in mouth
Do NOT restrain during seizure — protect from environmental hazards only
Time the seizure — if >5 minutes, administer midazolam
Temperature check immediately — rectal or axillary; 40.2°C is dangerously high
Active cooling — remove clothing; tepid sponge with lukewarm water (NOT ice); fan; cool environment
Oxygen via face mask or blow-by if SpO2 <94% or cyanosis
Blood glucose check — exclude hypoglycaemia as contributing factor
If seizure >5 minutes: Midazolam 0.2mg/kg intranasal (max 10mg) or 0.1mg/kg IM
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Febrile Seizure secondary to viral illness

allSummaries.title: Psychiatric - Acute Psychosis with Aggression
allSummaries.callReason: Son behaving erratically, breaking things, threatening family
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Apartment living room with broken furniture, male patient pacing and shouting
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young adult male, agitated, shouting incoherently
managementImmediate: Scene safety assessment BEFORE entry — identify exit routes, remove breakable objects if possible, request police backup if violence risk
Verbal de-escalation — calm voice, respectful tone, stand at an angle (not face-on), do not crowd patient; allow time — most escalation resolves with skilled communication
Maintain safe distance — remain beyond arm's reach until patient is calmer

Organic screen: blood glucose, SpO2, temperature, GCS — "behavioural change is organic until proven otherwise". Hyperthermia + diaphoresis + superhuman strength + bizarre speech + sudden tranquillity = Acute Behavioural Disturbance (ABD): medical emergency with risk of sudden cardiac death — continuous cardiac + temperature monitoring, NEVER prone restraint (positional asphyxia).
Structured suicide risk screen (Columbia-SSRS principles): document ideation, plan, means, intent, prior attempts, protective factors — all six domains.
Capacity assessment per UAE Federal Law 10/2023 (Mental Health Law) — 4-part test: can the patient understand, retain, weigh, and communicate the decision? Document. Least-restrictive principle.
Gather collateral history from family — medication history, previous episodes, recent drug/alcohol use

Chemical sedation only after verbal de-escalation fails AND organic causes excluded. Per NICE NG10: (1) IM lorazepam 1-2mg first-line if benzo-naive, (2) IM olanzapine 10mg, OR (3) IM haloperidol 5mg + PROMETHAZINE 25-50mg (never haloperidol alone — QT prolongation + EPSE risk; obtain 12-lead ECG before if possible). Avoid benzos in elderly delirium (paradoxical agitation).
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Acute Psychotic Episode - Bipolar Disorder
keyObservations: Agitated but not violent at present
redFlags: Could be medical emergency (head trauma, infection)

allSummaries.title: Toxicology - Organophosphate Poisoning
allSummaries.callReason: Worker collapsed after spraying pesticides, difficult breathing, vomiting
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Agricultural farm, patient found near pesticide spraying equipment
allSummaries.sceneImageCaption: Scene — Outdoor farm, hot sun, chemical smell in air
allSummaries.bystanders: 3 other workers with symptoms, farm supervisor
allSummaries.environment: Outdoor farm, hot sun, chemical smell in air
allSummaries.appearance: Diaphoretic, cyanotic, chemical odor on clothes
allSummaries.generalImpression: Critically ill male, vomiting, profuse sweating, difficulty breathing
managementImmediate: Scene safety - don full PPE before approaching patient
Remove contaminated clothing immediately
Decontaminate skin with soap and water (wet wipe if water unavailable)

Atropine 2mg IV/IM bolus — DOUBLE the dose every 3-5 minutes until secretions dry up (clear chest on auscultation, no bronchorrhoea). Titrate to DRYING of secretions ONLY — do NOT target heart rate or pupil size (mydriasis lags and is unreliable; tachycardia is expected from hypoxia/agitation). Total dose often exceeds 50mg in severe OP poisoning.
Pralidoxime (2-PAM) 1-2g IV over 30 minutes (if available)
High-flow oxygen and suction for secretions
IV access and fluid resuscitation
Prepare for airway compromise and respiratory failure
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Organophosphate Poisoning (Cholinergic Crisis)

allSummaries.title: Burns - Industrial Fire with Inhalation Injury
allSummaries.location: Industrial area in Jebel Ali, Dubai
allSummaries.callReason: Factory fire, multiple people trapped, one with severe burns
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Industrial factory with active fire, smoke throughout building, patient found near exit
allSummaries.appearance: Burns to face/neck/chest/arms, soot marks around nose/mouth
allSummaries.generalImpression: Adult male with extensive burns, conscious but in pain, coughing
managementImmediate: Stop the burning process — remove from heat source, remove smouldering clothing and jewellery (will continue to burn and become constricting as oedema forms)

Cool the burn with cool (NOT cold) running water for 20 minutes if within 3 hours of injury — cooling limited to burn site only; actively WARM the rest of the patient (hypothermia + large TBSA = lethal triad)
Dress with loose cling film applied lengthwise (never circumferential — constricts as oedema forms). Do NOT use wet dressings on large TBSA (hypothermia risk)
Assess airway - early intubation if soot around mouth/nose, hoarseness/stridor, facial burns, or singed nasal hairs
100% oxygen via non-rebreather (treat CO/CN poisoning)
IV access x2 with large-bore catheters
Fluid resuscitation: Parkland formula (4ml x weight(kg) x %TBSA, half in first 8 hours, half in next 16 hours)
Cover burns with sterile, dry, non-adherent dressing
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Major Thermal Burns with Inhalation Injury
keyObservations: Face/neck/chest burns - high risk for airway

allSummaries.title: Mass Casualty Incident - Bus vs Car Collision (8 Patients)
allSummaries.location: Sheikh Zayed Road, near Mall of Emirates, Dubai
allSummaries.callReason: Bus vs car collision, multiple injuries, road blocked, MCI declared
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Major RTC: Bus on side with significant damage, car severely damaged, debris scattered 50m across highway. Multiple victims visible. One patient trapped in car. Strong smell of fuel.
allSummaries.sceneImageCaption: Major RTC — bus vs car collision on highway
hazards: Fuel leak from bus tank - fire risk
Downed street light with exposed wires
Glass and metal debris across road
Traffic hazard - vehicles still passing on hard shoulder
Hot sun - risk of heat exhaustion for patients and responders
allSummaries.bystanders: Approximately 40 people: uninjured bus passengers, passing motorists, mall security
allSummaries.environment: Highway, exposed to sun, high ambient noise, chaotic
allSummaries.position: Various - some ambulatory, some seated, some supine
allSummaries.appearance: Variable - from walking wounded to critical trauma
allSummaries.generalImpression: MCI Scene - 8 patients visible requiring triage. Mixed injury severity. One patient unconscious. One patient trapped.
managementImmediate: Scene safety assessment — fuel leak, downed wires, unstable vehicles; do NOT enter until safe
Declare MCI immediately — call dispatch, request additional ambulances, fire, police, HEMS
Establish Incident Command Structure — designate Incident Commander, Triage Officer, Treatment Officer, Transport Officer
START triage — assess all 8 patients within 60 seconds each: Respiration, Perfusion, Mental Status
Apply colour-coded triage tags: RED (immediate), YELLOW (delayed), GREEN (minor), BLACK (expectant)
Life-saving interventions for RED patients only: airway adjuncts, haemorrhage control, chest decompression
Do NOT perform full ABCDE on each patient during triage — triage first, treat second
Establish helicopter landing zone if HEMS required
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Mass Casualty Incident - Multiple Trauma Patients
keyObservations: MCI with 8 distinct patients requiring individual assessment
START triage system must be implemented
RED (Immediate): 2 patients - airway compromise and severe hemorrhage
YELLOW (Delayed): 3 patients - significant but stable injuries
Multiple agencies needed: Ambulance, Fire, Police
redFlags: More RED priority patients than immediate transport capacity
Fuel leak presents fire and explosion risk
One patient trapped requiring prolonged extrication

allSummaries.title: Stable Angina - Exertional Chest Pain
allSummaries.callReason: Chest pain, not severe
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Shopping mall food court, air-conditioned
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly male, appears comfortable
managementImmediate: Obtain 12-lead ECG — within 10 minutes of arrival
Measure vital signs including blood pressure bilaterally
Detailed chest pain history using SOCRATES
Aspirin 300mg PO (crushed/chewed) if not already on daily aspirin and no contraindication
GTN spray 400mcg sublingual if SBP >90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor use in last 48 hours
IV access if pain persists or ECG changes present
Check blood glucose
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Stable Angina

allSummaries.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) - Young Adult
allSummaries.callReason: Heart racing, feels like going to pass out
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Modern apartment, patient sitting on sofa
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, anxious but stable
managementImmediate: Assess haemodynamic stability — BP, GCS, chest pain
Obtain 12-lead ECG to confirm narrow complex tachycardia
IV access (18G antecubital fossa)
If STABLE: Modified Valsalva manoeuvre — strain for 15 seconds supine, then raise legs to 45° for 15 seconds
If vagal fails: Adenosine 6mg rapid IV push with 20mL NS flush, monitor rhythm continuously
If no conversion after 1-2 minutes: Adenosine 12mg rapid IV push
If UNSTABLE (SBP <90, chest pain, GCS <14): Synchronized cardioversion 50-100J biphasic with sedation
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
redFlags: Pulse >180, needs vagal maneuvers or treatment
Young adult with SVT - common presentation

allSummaries.title: Acute Inferior STEMI with Right Ventricular Involvement
allSummaries.callReason: Severe chest pain, sweating, vomiting
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Hotel room, patient lying in bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged male, visibly distressed, diaphoretic
managementImmediate: 12-lead ECG immediately — identify inferior STE (II, III, aVF)
Right-sided ECG (V4R) — confirm RV infarction
DO NOT give nitrates — absolute contraindication in RV infarction
Keep patient SUPINE — do not sit up (preload dependent)

AVOID morphine / use fentanyl or very small titrated morphine (1-2mg) — morphine venodilates and can precipitate catastrophic hypotension in preload-dependent RV infarct; analgesia only if BP stable, reassess after each dose
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 94-98% (supplement only if <94%)
IV access x2 (14-16G)
Aspirin 300mg PO (crushed/chewed)
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Acute Inferior STEMI with Right Ventricular Infarction
keyObservations: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF ST elevation)
redFlags: Vomiting with inferior MI = large infarct

allSummaries.title: Chest Pain with Known LBBB - Possible Occlusion MI
allSummaries.callReason: Chest pain, shortness of breath
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Apartment, patient in armchair with oxygen
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly male, respiratory distress, clutching chest
managementImmediate: 12-lead ECG immediately — identify LBBB pattern (wide QRS, dominant S in V1, broad R in V5-V6)
Apply Sgarbossa criteria to assess for MI: concordant ST elevation ≥1mm, concordant ST depression V1-V3, or excessively discordant STE ≥5mm
Treat as STEMI equivalent if Sgarbossa positive or new/presumed new LBBB with chest pain
High-flow oxygen 15L/min if SpO2 <94%
IV access x2 (14-16G)
Aspirin 300mg PO
GTN only if SBP >90 mmHg — may help acute heart failure
Patient upright to assist breathing
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Myocardial Infarction with LBBB (Sgarbossa Criteria Positive)
redFlags: New or presumed new LBBB with chest pain = STEMI equivalent
Sgarbossa criteria = MI until proven otherwise

allSummaries.title: Atrial Flutter with 2:1 Block - Elderly Patient
allSummaries.callReason: Heart racing, feeling weak
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Nursing home room, patient in bed
allSummaries.generalImpression: Elderly female, slightly anxious but stable
managementImmediate: Assess haemodynamic stability — BP, GCS, chest pain
Obtain 12-lead ECG — identify sawtooth flutter waves in II, III, aVF at ~300 bpm
IV access (18G)

If STABLE: prehospital focus is continuous monitoring, IV access, identifying precipitants. Rate-control agents (metoprolol 5mg IV or diltiazem 0.25mg/kg IV) are ED-administered — not within UK JRCALC / UAE DCAS paramedic scope. Transport under monitoring.
Check anticoagulation status — warfarin INR range?
Identify precipitant — missed medication dose confirmed; check electrolytes if available
If UNSTABLE (SBP <90 or haemodynamic compromise): Synchronized cardioversion 50-100J biphasic
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Atrial Flutter with 2:1 Block
redFlags: Atrial flutter can degenerate into atrial fibrillation

allSummaries.title: Syncope - Rule Out Cardiac Cause

Full vital signs including orthostatic BP (lying, sitting, standing with 1-2 min between positions)
Check blood glucose — hypoglycaemia is a reversible cause
Obtain 12-lead ECG — mandatory in all syncope presentations
IV access if ongoing symptoms or abnormal ECG
Detailed history of syncopal event: prodrome, position, duration, post-ictal state, witnesses
Family history of sudden cardiac death

Need to check for orthostatic changes

allSummaries.title: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure - "Crashing Asthma"
allSummaries.callReason: Cannot breathe, asthma attack
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Apartment, patient sitting on edge of bed leaning forward

allSummaries.title: Severe Hyperkalemia with ECG Changes

allSummaries.generalImpression: Middle-aged male, appears weak, muscle weakness
managementImmediate: 12-lead ECG immediately — identify hyperkalemia pattern: peaked T waves, wide QRS, loss of P waves, sine wave

Cardiac monitoring continuous — sine wave = pre-arrest, prepare for immediate intervention
Calcium gluconate 10% 10mL (1g) IV over 2-3 minutes — cardioprotection, stabilises myocardial membrane
Or Calcium chloride 10% 5-10mL IV via central line if available — 3x more ionised calcium

allSummaries.title: Drowning with Hypothermia
allSummaries.callReason: Child pulled from swimming pool, not breathing
allSummaries.sceneDescription: Poolside, child on towel
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young child, pale, not breathing
managementImmediate: Rescue from water safely — do not enter dangerous water without trained water rescue; use reach and throw techniques
C-spine precautions if dive/fall mechanism — log roll for spinal management during rescue if safe to do so
Airway suctioning — water and vomit in upper airway; use rigid suction catheter
Drowning is ASPHYXIAL arrest — start with 5 RESCUE BREATHS before compressions (ERC / Resus Council UK drowning algorithm). Then reassess for signs of life.
Assess for respiratory effort and pulse — up to 60 seconds for hypothermic pulse check
If no pulse or apnoea after rescue breaths — CPR immediately. Paediatric ratio 15:2 (two rescuers), depth 1/3 AP chest diameter (~4-5cm), rate 100-120/min. Adult 30:2.
High-flow oxygen 15L/min via NRB or BVM — SpO2 83% is critically low
Remove wet clothing — wet clothing accelerates heat loss
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Drowning with Hypothermia

allSummaries.title: Electrical Burn with Cardiac Arrest

Advanced airway — RSI or supraglottic airway; electrical burns can cause airway oedema rapidly
IV/IO access — large bore bilateral antecubital fossa
Adrenaline 1mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes per ALS algorithm
Examine for entry and exit wounds — entry typically at contact point (hands), exit where current left body (feet)
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Electrical Injury with Cardiac Arrest

Mental health crisis requires assessment and support

allSummaries.title: Inferior STEMI with Right Ventricular Infarction

managementImmediate: STOP all nitrates — absolutely contraindicated in RV infarct
Keep SUPINE — do NOT sit patient up
High-flow oxygen 15L/min
IV access x2
Cautious 250mL NS bolus — monitor for fluid overload

Morphine 2.5mg IV titrated for pain (avoid large doses — may worsen hypotension)

ST elevation in V1 suggesting RV involvement
Clear lungs despite significant hypotension (RV failure, not LV)
First-degree AV block (common in inferior MI)
redFlags: Risk of complete heart block (inferior MI can progress)
Bradycardia with potential for hemodynamic collapse

Loss of P waves — atrial standstill

allSummaries.consciousness: Alert but unable to speak — single words only
allSummaries.generalImpression: Young female, severe respiratory distress, can only speak single words, exhausting
managementImmediate: REMOVE TRIGGER — eliminate incense and any smoke from environment immediately
Position upright — Fowler's or tripod; NEVER lay flat; gravity-assisted respiration critical
High-flow oxygen 15L/min via non-rebreather mask — target SpO2 >94%; hypoxia is the killer
Salbutamol 5mg nebulised CONTINUOUSLY — repeat every 15-20 minutes or continuous if deteriorating
Ipratropium 500mcg nebulised — combine with salbutamol for maximum bronchodilation
IV access x2 (14-16G antecubital) — prepare for IV drugs and fluids
Hydrocortisone 200mg IV immediately — inflammation reduction is essential
Adrenaline 0.5mg IM (1:1000) if life-threatening features develop — bronchospasm unresponsive to above
allSummaries.mostLikelyDiagnosis: Severe Asthma Exacerbation
keyObservations: Salbutamol alone will NOT resolve this
redFlags: Diminished air entry suggests severe obstruction
If gets silent chest = imminent arrest
